summary: The article describes EBT-101, a one-dose CRISPR-Cas9 gene therapy for HIV now in the first human clinical trial of a gene-editing HIV treatment. Early results from three patients show no toxic effects or serious adverse events, but it is not yet known whether it cures HIV. Experts caution that off-target effects may take years to appear and that treatment interruption tests are needed to show whether latent HIV reservoirs are disabled.
one_line: An early human trial of the CRISPR therapy EBT-101 shows initial safety for HIV, but whether it can cure the infection remains unknown.
key_facts: EBT-101 is a CRISPR-Cas9 gene therapy for HIV; this is the first time a gene-editing treatment for HIV has been tried in humans.
CRISPR-Cas9 was developed in 2012, and the approach has been studied in animal models since then.
UNAIDS reports about 39 million people were living with HIV in 2022, with about 630,000 AIDS-related deaths that year.
Combination antiretroviral therapies (cARTs) extend lives to near-normal lengths but must be taken for a lifetime and are not a cure.
Latent HIV persists in CD4+ memory T cells, which can persist for decades, and dormant proviruses can reactivate if cART is interrupted.
EBT-101 uses multiple guides to target multiple genome sites and snip out large sections of latently integrated HIV DNA.
Kamel Khalili of Temple University, co-founder of Excision BioTherapeutics, has worked on developing EBT-101 for a decade.
Khalili's team published reports in 2020 and 2023 showing that EBT-100, a precursor, safely removed HIV DNA in infected primates.
Initial results from three treated patients showed no toxic effects or serious adverse events, and all patients' HIV is suppressed with cART.
Thomas Hope warns that genetic off-target mutations can take years to manifest as complications.
The trial will next test additional EBT-101 doses for safety, then check whether the virus stays suppressed when patients are taken off cART.
Participants will be enrolled in a 15-year long-term follow-up study after their initial dose.
A handful of people have been effectively cured of HIV through intensive stem-cell transplants.
